subChunks.title: Forensic Genealogy Principles & Practice

storyBeats.txt: Forensic genealogy, Theodora said, leaning forward, is genealogy with stakes. A court case. An estate worth millions. A cold-case murder. A living person who has no idea they're being searched for.
The methods are the same DNA, documents, logic. What changes is the burden of proof, the ethics, and the consequences of error. You are no longer just curious. You are accountable.

The discipline splits into two branches: heir hunting, where you locate missing beneficiaries of estates, and investigative genetic genealogy, where you use DNA to identify unknown individuals — living or deceased — for law enforcement.

Both branches require the same rigorous documentation the GPS demands. The difference is that in forensic work, your research may end up in a courtroom, and your methods will be scrutinised by opposing counsel.

subChunks.hookHtml:
In 2018, investigators in California uploaded crime-scene DNA from the Golden State Killer to GEDmatch — a public genealogy database — and identified a suspect through distant cousins. Joseph James DeAngelo, who had murdered thirteen people, was arrested within months. Forensic genealogy had moved from obscure niche to front-page news overnight.

The case transformed the discipline. It demonstrated that genetic genealogy could solve cold cases where all other methods had failed. It also raised profound questions about consent, privacy, and the proper boundaries between genealogical research and law enforcement surveillance. Forensic genealogy is now a recognised profession, with its own certification pathways, ethical codes, and court-tested standards.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What Is Forensic Genealogy?

Forensic genealogy applies genealogical research methods to legal contexts. The two principal branches are:

  • Heir location (probate genealogy): Identifying and locating living heirs to estates where beneficiaries are unknown, missing, or their relationship to the deceased is uncertain. Work may be commissioned by solicitors, probate courts, or estate administrators.
  • Investigative genetic genealogy (IGG): Using DNA uploaded to genealogical databases to identify unknown individuals — typically unidentified human remains or suspects in serious criminal cases. Work is normally commissioned by law enforcement agencies.

Heir Location: The Evidence Standard

Heir location requires constructing a full pedigree of the deceased and tracing all lines of descent to locate qualifying heirs. The work must satisfy legal evidentiary standards — in England and Wales this typically means satisfying a solicitor and sometimes a court that the research is complete and the conclusions reliable.

Key documentation practices include: citing every source used; distinguishing between proven relationships and inferred ones; preparing a narrative report with pedigree charts; and retaining all working notes in case of later challenge. The Society of Genealogists and AGRA both publish standards for heir-location work.

Bona Vacantia is the doctrine governing English estates where no heirs can be found — assets pass to the Crown. The Bona Vacantia Division (BVD) publishes a list of unclaimed estates (gov.uk/government/collections/bona-vacantia); heir hunters may approach these commercially, taking a percentage of the inheritance as their fee from any located heirs.

Investigative Genetic Genealogy (IGG)

IGG begins with a DNA profile — either from crime-scene evidence or from unidentified remains — uploaded to a public genealogical database. GEDmatch and FamilyTreeDNA have both adopted opt-in consent policies for law enforcement use following the Golden State Killer controversy.

The workflow: (1) Upload the unknown profile; (2) Identify the highest-cM matches; (3) Build trees for those matches working backwards and then forward to identify descendants living in the right time and place; (4) Narrow the candidate list using age, geography, sex, and other corroborating information; (5) Submit a candidate name to law enforcement, who then obtain a confirmatory reference sample through conventional investigation.

The genealogist's role ends at providing a candidate list — arrest and prosecution are law enforcement functions. This separation is ethically critical.

The Parabon NanoLabs Model

Parabon NanoLabs became the dominant commercial IGG provider after the Golden State Killer case. Their workflow combines SNP phenotyping (predicting physical appearance from DNA) with genealogical tree-building. They maintain that their genealogists work only on cases involving violent crimes or unidentified remains — not property crimes or immigration enforcement — a policy boundary that has become an industry norm.

Ethical Constraints and Consent

IGG raises ethical issues that conventional genealogy does not. When you build a family tree to identify an unknown profile, you are exposing the DNA of people — relatives of the unknown individual — who consented only to genealogical use of their data. The DNA of a third-degree cousin can narrow a suspect list to a handful of people.

The ISOGG, Association of Professional Genealogists (APG), and National Center for Forensic Science have all published guidelines. The consensus holds that IGG should be limited to: violent crimes (homicide, sexual assault); unidentified remains; and only as a last resort after other investigative methods have been exhausted. Use for property crimes, immigration enforcement, or civil disputes is widely condemned.

GEDmatch's 2019 policy change — switching from opt-out to opt-in for law enforcement matching — dramatically reduced the database's utility for IGG but strengthened participant consent. The debate over the correct balance continues.

Court Admissibility

Genealogical evidence in courts must satisfy the relevant jurisdiction's standards. In the US, expert witness testimony is governed by the Daubert standard: the methodology must be scientifically valid, reliably applied, and relevant to the facts. Genealogists offering expert testimony must demonstrate their qualifications, cite their sources, and be prepared for cross-examination on their methods.

In the UK, expert witnesses must comply with Civil Procedure Rules Part 35 (CPR 35) or equivalent criminal procedure rules, and their overriding duty is to the court, not to the instructing party.

Professional Credentials

The Board for Certification of Genealogists (BCG) offers the Certified Genealogist (CG) credential — the primary route for forensic genealogists needing a recognised professional credential in the US. The Genealogical Proof Standard is the quality benchmark. AGRA (Association of Genealogists and Researchers in Archives) serves equivalent functions in the UK. Some universities now offer graduate certificate programmes specifically in forensic genealogy.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a curious 16-year-old how a genealogist can help identify a crime suspect using DNA from distant cousins — without having the suspect's DNA at all.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
An estate solicitor contacts you about a client who died intestate (without a will), leaving a house valued at £400,000. The deceased, Arthur Blackwood (1938–2023), never married and had no known children. The solicitor needs to identify all living heirs. Arthur's parents were William Blackwood (1905–1961) and Edna née Marsh (1910–1975). They had three children: Arthur, a daughter Violet (1936–1989), and a son George (1940–2019).

Outline the heir-location research process: what records would you consult to trace Violet's and George's descendants, and what would constitute adequate proof of relationship for the solicitor?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
The research must trace every living descendant of William and Edna. Starting with Violet (1936–1989): locate her death certificate (confirming parentage if possible), marriage certificate(s), and birth registrations of her children. Then trace each of Violet's children forward: their marriages and their children, through to the present day. Repeat for George (1940–2019) and his descendants.

Key records: GRO births/marriages/deaths (certified copies); 1939 Register (ages of parents, siblings); census returns 1939; electoral registers (tracing addresses over time); probate records for Arthur, Violet, George (wills name family members); family history sources such as family trees cross-referenced against documents.

Proof of relationship requires documentary evidence at each generational step — a birth certificate naming both parents, or a marriage certificate naming parents, linking each descendant back to William and Edna. Inference is not sufficient; each link must be documented. The final report should contain a narrative, fully cited sources, pedigree chart, and a clear statement of which relationships are proven and which (if any) remain uncertain.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Evaluate the ethical arguments for and against law enforcement use of public genealogical DNA databases (like GEDmatch) to identify suspects in serious crimes. Consider: the rights of database users who consented to genealogical use; the rights of crime victims and their families; the interests of society in solving violent crimes; and the risk of function creep (extending IGG to less serious crimes). Where should the ethical line be drawn, and how should it be enforced?
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The strongest argument for IGG use is consequentialist: it solves violent crimes that would otherwise remain unsolved, brings justice to victims' families, and prevents future harm by identifying dangerous offenders. The Golden State Killer had murdered for decades with impunity; IGG succeeded where decades of conventional investigation had failed.

Against this, database users consented to genealogical matching, not criminal investigation. Their DNA exposes the genetic privacy of all their relatives, most of whom never consented to anything. This is a form of third-party surveillance by proxy. Moreover, if law enforcement access is permitted, scope creep becomes a genuine risk — beginning with murder and expanding to lesser offences, or eventually to immigration enforcement or civil disputes.

A defensible position holds that IGG is justified only when: (a) the crime is a violent felony or involves unidentified remains; (b) conventional investigation has been exhausted; (c) law enforcement has obtained appropriate legal authority; (d) the database used operates on opt-in consent for law enforcement. This mirrors the policies of GEDmatch post-2019 and FamilyTreeDNA. Enforcement is best achieved through professional codes of conduct (APG, ISOGG guidelines), contractual terms between databases and law enforcement agencies, and statutory regulation.

The strongest counterargument to restriction is that opt-in consent dramatically reduces database size and thus utility — effectively limiting IGG to cases where the suspect's relatives have actively consented to law enforcement use, which may be a vanishingly small subset. Balancing these interests is a live policy debate, not a resolved one.
learningObjectives: Distinguish the two main branches of forensic genealogy and their respective client bases.
Describe the investigative genetic genealogy workflow from DNA upload to candidate identification.
Evaluate the ethical constraints governing law enforcement use of public genealogical databases.
Explain the documentation and reporting standards required for heir-location work to satisfy legal proceedings.
commonMistakes: Conflating the genealogist's role (identifying candidates) with law enforcement's role (investigation and arrest).
Using IGG for cases that do not meet the violent-crime threshold — a serious ethical breach.
Treating GEDmatch matches as proof of identity rather than as a starting point for documentary verification.
Failing to document working notes in heir-location cases, leaving conclusions unchallengeable if disputed later.
assessmentCriteria: Accurately distinguishes heir location from investigative genetic genealogy, including their different client bases and standards.
Demonstrates understanding of the IGG workflow and the crucial separation between genealogical candidate identification and law enforcement action.
Engages critically with consent and privacy ethics, acknowledging the interests of database users, victims, and society.
Applies GPS-level documentation standards to forensic heir-location work.

questions.questionHtml: In investigative genetic genealogy (IGG), at what point does the genealogist's role typically end?
options: When a candidate name or list is submitted to law enforcement
When the DNA match exceeds 500 cM
When a court has accepted the genealogical evidence
questions.correctAnswer: When a candidate name or list is submitted to law enforcement
questions.explanationHtml: The genealogist identifies candidates from DNA matches and documentary evidence; arrest, investigation, and prosecution are entirely law enforcement functions. This separation is ethically essential.

questions.questionHtml: You are conducting heir-location research for a solicitor. Arthur died intestate; you have documented his sister Violet's two children but cannot find any record of whether Violet's elder son ever married or had children. How should you handle this gap in your report?
options: Assume he had no children and proceed with the remaining heirs
Note the gap explicitly, describe the records searched, and state that the research is incomplete pending further investigation
Omit him from the pedigree since unconfirmed relationships cannot be included
Mark him as deceased without evidence and distribute the estate among the confirmed heirs
questions.correctAnswer: Note the gap explicitly, describe the records searched, and state that the research is incomplete pending further investigation
questions.explanationHtml: Heir-location reports must be transparent about what is known, what is unknown, and what records have been searched. Assuming the absence of heirs without documentary proof could lead to incorrect distribution of the estate and legal liability.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following uses of investigative genetic genealogy is most widely condemned by professional genealogical organisations?
options: Identifying an unknown murder victim from DNA found at a scene
Identifying a suspect in a decades-old unsolved homicide case
Using IGG to identify undocumented immigrants for deportation proceedings
Identifying unidentified remains from a mass disaster
questions.correctAnswer: Using IGG to identify undocumented immigrants for deportation proceedings
questions.explanationHtml: Professional consensus (APG, ISOGG) limits IGG to violent crimes and unidentified remains. Applying it to immigration enforcement is widely condemned as function creep that violates the consent under which database users submitted their DNA.
